Exercise A

Two Roads to Freedom

Read the text carefully, then answer the comprehension questions using the dropdown menus.

Reading Text

By the 1950s, Black Americans in the southern United States still lived under segregation laws separating them from white citizens in schools, buses and restaurants. In 1955, Rosa Parks refused to give up her bus seat to a white passenger in Montgomery, Alabama, sparking a year-long boycott that launched Martin Luther King Jr. into the national spotlight.

King believed lasting change could only be achieved through nonviolent resistance. Inspired partly by Gandhi, he organised peaceful marches, sit-ins and boycotts, arguing that suffering endured without retaliation would eventually shame the nation into reform. His famous "I Have a Dream" speech, delivered in 1963, called for a future in which people would be judged by their character, not their skin colour.

Malcolm X took a very different view. Having grown up amid poverty and racism, he grew frustrated with the slow pace of change and argued that Black Americans should defend themselves "by any means necessary" rather than wait patiently for equality. Whereas King appealed to white America's conscience, Malcolm X focused on Black pride, self-reliance and economic independence, insisting that real power would never simply be given away.

Although their strategies diverged sharply, both men were assassinated within a few years of each other, and both are now honoured as central figures of the civil rights era. Their contrasting approaches still shape debates today, including within the Black Lives Matter movement, which draws on King's tradition of peaceful protest while echoing Malcolm X's insistence on urgency and self-determination.

Exercise D

Writing — Comparing Two Approaches

Write a comment (6–8 sentences) comparing Martin Luther King's and Malcolm X's approaches to civil rights. Say which approach you find more convincing and why. Use at least four linking words from Exercise B (e.g. however, whereas, on the other hand, furthermore, although, in contrast).
